tips.title: Continuo first, dynamics second
tips.body: For an unfamiliar piece, ask two questions in order. **Is there a continuo?** A harpsichord under a bass line means Baroque. **Are the dynamics terraced or gradual?** Steps mean Baroque, a crescendo means Classical. Those two usually settle it.

tips.title: The instrument explains the dynamics
tips.body: A harpsichord quill plucks with the **same force** however hard you press, so a crescendo is impossible and dynamics must be **terraced**. The piano's hammers make touch matter — which is why it is called the **pianoforte**, meaning *soft-loud*.

tips.title: Rondo or ritornello?
tips.body: Both alternate a recurring idea with episodes, so the **key** decides. A **rondo**'s A stays in the **tonic** and returns unchanged: Classical. A **ritornello** returns in **different keys** and is often **shortened**: Baroque.

tips.title: A sonata is not sonata form
tips.body: A **sonata** is a whole piece, usually in three or four movements. **Sonata form** is the shape of a **single movement**, usually the first — and it is used in symphonies, quartets and concertos too.

tips.title: Both subjects come home
tips.body: In the **exposition** the two subjects are in **different keys**. In the **recapitulation** both are in the **tonic**. That return is the whole point of sonata form, and it is what makes the ending sound final.

steps.title: Why these dates, and what changed
steps.body:
**Area of Study 1 is Instrumental Music 1700 to 1820**, and the dates are not arbitrary. They cover the **last fifty years of the Baroque period** and the **whole of the Classical period**.

- **Baroque**: roughly **1600 to 1750**. The end date is the year **Bach died**.
- **Classical**: roughly **1750 to 1820**.

So this area of study is really **two styles**, not one, and almost every question about it comes down to telling them apart.

**The two set works sit at either end.** Bach's **Brandenburg Concerto No. 5** was dedicated to the Margrave of Brandenburg in **1721**, firmly Baroque. Beethoven's **Pathétique** sonata was composed in **1798**, firmly Classical — and looking forward to what came next. The two are **seventy-seven years apart**, and the music changed enormously in between.

**Instrumental music** means music **without voices**. That is the other half of the definition, and it is what separates this area of study from Area of Study 2, Vocal Music.

**The single biggest change across these dates** is what the music is built out of. Baroque music is typically built from **counterpoint** — independent lines woven together. Classical music is typically built from **melody and accompaniment** — one tune on top, support underneath. Everything else in this topic follows from that shift.

steps.title: Telling Baroque from Classical
steps.body:
This is the comparison to know cold, because a question on an **unfamiliar** piece from this area of study is really asking which of the two it is.

**Texture.** Baroque music is often **polyphonic** or **contrapuntal** — several independent lines of equal importance. Classical music is mostly **homophonic**: a clear melody with accompaniment beneath it.

**Dynamics.** Baroque music uses **terraced dynamics** — sudden changes between loud and soft, like steps, with no gradual change in between. Classical music uses **crescendo and diminuendo**, growing and fading. This is the easiest difference to hear.

**The continuo.** Baroque music nearly always has a **basso continuo**: a bass line played by a cello or bassoon, with a **harpsichord or organ** filling in the chords above it from a **figured bass** — numbers under the bass line telling the player which chords to use. By the Classical period the continuo has **disappeared**. If you can hear a harpsichord chugging away underneath, it is Baroque.

**Melody.** Baroque melodies tend to be long, **spun out** and highly **ornamented**, often unfolding continuously without obvious stopping points. Classical melodies are **balanced and periodic** — tidy phrases, often in answering pairs of two or four bars.

**Harmony.** Baroque harmony drives forward with strong **sequences** and frequent movement. Classical harmony is **simpler and slower-moving**, which leaves the melody exposed on top.

**Keyboard.** Baroque means **harpsichord**. Classical means **piano**. The next step explains why that one change drives several of the others.

steps.title: From harpsichord to piano
steps.body:
One instrument changing explains a surprising amount of this period.

**The harpsichord plucks.** Pressing a key makes a quill pluck the string. A quill plucks with the **same force every time**, so **however hard you press, the volume does not change**. A harpsichord cannot make a crescendo. To get louder or softer, a player changes manual or adds a stop — which produces a **sudden step**, and that is exactly what **terraced dynamics** are. The dynamics of Baroque music are, in part, the dynamics the instrument could physically produce.

**The piano strikes.** Around **1700** Bartolomeo Cristofori built a keyboard whose hammers **strike** the strings and fall away. Strike harder and you get a louder note. That is why its full name is **pianoforte**: *soft-loud*, the thing the harpsichord could not do.

**So the piano makes gradual dynamics possible**, and Classical composers write them. The expressive shaping of a Mozart or Beethoven melody depends on an instrument that can grow and fade.

**Beethoven's Pathétique is a good example of the consequence.** The very title — *Grande Sonate Pathétique* — promises feeling, and the piece opens with dramatic contrasts of loud and soft that no harpsichord could play.

**The orchestra changed too.** A Baroque orchestra was mostly **strings plus continuo**, with wind instruments added as required. By the Classical period the orchestra had **standardised**: strings, **pairs** of woodwind — flutes, oboes, clarinets, bassoons — with horns, trumpets and timpani. The **clarinet** is a Classical arrival; you will not find one in Bach.

steps.title: The Baroque concerto: ritornello form
steps.body:
A **concerto** sets a soloist, or a small group of soloists, against a larger ensemble. In the Baroque there are **two kinds**, and the difference is simply how many soloists there are.

- **Concerto grosso** — a **small group** of soloists, called the **concertino**, against the full ensemble, called the **ripieno** or **tutti**. Handel's *Concerto Grosso op 6 no. 5* is one, and so is Bach's **Brandenburg Concerto No. 5**, where the concertino is flute, violin and harpsichord.
- **Solo concerto** — **one** soloist against the ensemble. Vivaldi's *Winter*, from *The Four Seasons*, is one.

**Both use ritornello form.** *Ritornello* means *little return*. A **tutti** passage — the ritornello — comes back again and again between **episodes** played by the soloists.

$$\text{Ritornello} \rightarrow \text{episode} \rightarrow \text{ritornello} \rightarrow \text{episode} \rightarrow \text{ritornello}$$

Two details make it more than a simple alternation:

- The ritornello usually comes back **in different keys** as the movement proceeds, returning to the tonic at the end.
- It is often **shortened** on its later appearances, so the returns are recognisable without being literal.

**Why it exists.** Before the piano, dynamics were terraced, so the most effective contrast available was **between groups of players** — few against many. Ritornello form is built out of exactly that contrast, and it is why the Baroque concerto sounds the way it does.

steps.title: Sonata form
steps.body:
**Sonata form** is the most important Classical structure, and it is the form of the **first movement of Beethoven's Pathétique** and of **Mozart's Piano Sonata in C, K.545**. It has three main parts.

**1. Exposition** — the ideas are stated.

- **First subject**, in the **tonic** key.
- A **transition**, or bridge, which changes key.
- **Second subject**, in a **new key**: the **dominant** if the piece is in a major key, or the **relative major** if it is in a minor key.
- The exposition is usually **repeated**.

**2. Development** — the ideas are taken apart. Fragments of the subjects are broken up, combined, and passed through **distant keys**. This is the least stable and most dramatic part, and it is where a composer shows what the material can do.

**3. Recapitulation** — the ideas return. Both subjects come back, but now **both in the tonic**. That is the crucial change: the second subject, which was in a different key, is brought home.

There may also be a slow **introduction** before the exposition — the *Pathétique* has a famous one — and a **coda** to finish.

$$\text{Exposition} \rightarrow \text{Development} \rightarrow \text{Recapitulation}$$

**The single thing to remember**: in the exposition the two subjects are in **different keys**; in the recapitulation they are in **the same key**. Sonata form is a journey away from home and back, and the return is what makes the ending feel final.

**Do not confuse a sonata with sonata form.** A **sonata** is a *piece*, usually in three or four movements for one or two instruments. **Sonata form** is the *shape of one movement* — usually the first. A sonata's first movement is normally in sonata form, but so is the first movement of most Classical symphonies, quartets and concertos.

steps.title: The other structures, and the Alberti bass
steps.body:
Besides sonata form and ritornello form, four structures come up repeatedly in this area of study.

- **Binary form: A B.** Two sections, each usually repeated. A moves from the tonic to a related key; B comes back. Common in Baroque dances.
- **Ternary form: A B A.** A middle section that contrasts, then the opening returns.
- **Minuet and trio.** A ternary design at a larger scale: the minuet, then a contrasting trio, then the minuet again. Standard as the third movement of a Classical symphony or quartet. The *trio* is so called because it was once played by three instruments.
- **Rondo: A B A C A.** One idea keeps coming back, unchanged, with contrasting episodes between. The third movement of Haydn's *English Sonata* is a rondo, and a rondo is a common Classical **finale** — it is cheerful and easy to follow, which suits a last movement.
- **Theme and variations.** A theme, then repeated versions altered in melody, harmony, rhythm, texture or key.

**Rondo against ritornello** is worth being careful about, because they sound similar in description. In a **rondo**, the recurring **A section stays in the tonic** and returns essentially unchanged. In **ritornello form**, the ritornello **changes key** and is often **shortened**. Rondo is Classical; ritornello is Baroque.

**The Alberti bass.** This is a small thing worth knowing because it is a giveaway. It is an accompaniment pattern made from a broken chord played **lowest, highest, middle, highest**, over and over, in the left hand. It gives a steady, gentle background that lets the right-hand melody sing, and it is **characteristically Classical** — you can hear it in Mozart's K.545. It is the sound of homophony: the accompaniment busy but subordinate, the tune clearly on top.

steps.title: The wider listening, and what each piece is for
steps.body:
For this area of study Pearson suggests four **wider listening** pieces. They are **not compulsory**, and a teacher may choose others. Their purpose is to give **background and context** to the set works, and — importantly for the exam — to prepare you for the **unfamiliar** pieces you will meet in Section A and Section B.

| Composer | Work | What it shows |
|---|---|---|
| **G F Handel** | Concerto Grosso op 6 no. 5, second movement | the **concerto grosso**, and ritornello form |
| **A Vivaldi** | *Winter*, from *The Four Seasons* | the **solo concerto**, and Baroque word-painting |
| **W A Mozart** | Piano Sonata in C major, K.545, first movement | **sonata form**, and the Alberti bass |
| **F J Haydn** | Piano Sonata in C major, the *English Sonata*, Hob 50, third movement | **rondo** form as a Classical finale |

**Notice how the four are arranged.** Two Baroque and two Classical; two concertos and two keyboard sonatas; and between them the four structures this area of study rests on. They are not a random list — they cover the ground the set works do not.

**Why this matters for the exam.** The specification requires that work on **each** area of study includes wider listening, because **one Section A question is on an unfamiliar piece** with a skeleton score, and the **Section B extended response compares a set work with an unfamiliar piece from the same area of study**. You cannot revise the unfamiliar piece. What you can do is know the **style** well enough that an unfamiliar piece in it holds no surprises.

steps.title: Going deeper: why the music changed
steps.body:
**Do not just list the differences — explain them.** The Baroque-to-Classical shift was not a change of fashion, and an answer that can say **why** reads very differently from one that recites a table.

**The instrument came first.** The harpsichord plucks with the same force however hard you press, so gradual dynamics are physically impossible on it and dynamics have to be **terraced**. Cristofori's hammer action, from around 1700, made touch-sensitive playing possible, and the **pianoforte** is named for exactly that. Once a keyboard could grow and fade, composers wrote music that grows and fades — and a texture with a **singing melody on top** is the one that benefits most. So the piano and homophony arrive together.

**The continuo disappeared for a related reason.** A continuo exists to fill in the harmony. Once the harmony is spelled out in the parts themselves — in an Alberti bass, or in sustained wind chords — nothing is left for it to fill in. The Classical orchestra made the continuo redundant rather than unfashionable.

**Form followed texture.** Ritornello form is built on the contrast between **few players and many**, which was the strongest contrast available when dynamics were terraced. Once gradual dynamics, a standardised orchestra and clear melody-and-accompaniment textures existed, a different kind of contrast became possible: **contrast of key and of theme**. That is what sonata form is built on. The forms changed because the available contrasts changed.

**The audience changed too.** Baroque instrumental music was written largely for courts and churches; by the Classical period there was a growing public concert life and a market for amateurs to play at home. Music that is **balanced, periodic and easy to follow** suits a paying public and an amateur pianist. Mozart's K.545 is a teaching sonata.

**For the unfamiliar-piece questions**, work in this order: **continuo or not**, then **dynamics**, then **texture**, then **keyboard**. The first two usually settle it, and the others confirm. Say what you heard and what it tells you — *a harpsichord realising a figured bass, so this is Baroque* — rather than naming a period and hoping.

**For Section B**, remember you are comparing a set work with an unfamiliar piece **from the same area of study**. So the comparison is likely to be Baroque against Classical, or two works in the same style. Either way, the six elements in step 2 give you a ready-made structure, and using the same element on both pieces in turn is what makes a comparison a comparison rather than two descriptions.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Area of Study 1: Instrumental Music 1700 to 1820.** Instrumental means **without voices**.
- It covers the **last fifty years of the Baroque** (about 1600 to 1750) and **all of the Classical** (about 1750 to 1820).
- The set works are **Bach's Brandenburg Concerto No. 5**, dedicated **1721**, and **Beethoven's Pathétique**, composed **1798**.
- **Baroque**: polyphonic, terraced dynamics, **basso continuo** with figured bass, long ornamented melodies, driving sequences, **harpsichord**.
- **Classical**: homophonic, **crescendo and diminuendo**, no continuo, balanced periodic phrases, simpler harmony, **piano**.
- The **harpsichord plucks**, so touch cannot change the volume — which is why Baroque dynamics are **terraced**.
- The **piano strikes**, so it can. Its full name, **pianoforte**, means *soft-loud*.
- Baroque orchestra: mostly **strings plus continuo**. Classical orchestra: strings, **pairs of woodwind**, horns, trumpets, timpani. The **clarinet** is a Classical arrival.
- **Concerto grosso**: a small group of soloists, the **concertino**, against the **ripieno**. **Solo concerto**: one soloist.
- **Ritornello form**: a tutti ritornello alternating with solo episodes, returning in **different keys** and often **shortened**.
- **Sonata form**: **exposition** (first subject in the tonic, transition, second subject in the dominant or relative major), **development**, **recapitulation** (both subjects **in the tonic**).
- A **sonata** is a piece; **sonata form** is the shape of one movement.
- **Binary** is A B; **ternary** is A B A; **minuet and trio** is ternary at a larger scale; **rondo** is A B A C A.
- **Rondo against ritornello**: a rondo's A stays in the **tonic** and returns unchanged; a ritornello **changes key** and is **shortened**.
- An **Alberti bass** is a broken chord played lowest, highest, middle, highest — characteristically **Classical**.
- **Wider listening**: Handel's *Concerto Grosso op 6 no. 5*, Vivaldi's *Winter*, Mozart's **K.545**, Haydn's *English Sonata*. Suggestions, not compulsory.

questions.prompt: Compare Baroque and Classical instrumental style, using at least five musical elements.
questions.solution: Baroque instrumental music, written roughly between 1600 and 1750, differs from Classical music of about 1750 to 1820 across every element. In texture, Baroque music is typically polyphonic or contrapuntal, with several independent lines of equal importance woven together, whereas Classical music is predominantly homophonic, with a clear melody and a subordinate accompaniment beneath it, often an Alberti bass in keyboard music. In dynamics, the Baroque uses terraced dynamics, sudden steps between loud and soft with no gradual change, while Classical composers write crescendos and diminuendos. Baroque music almost always includes a basso continuo, a bass line played by cello or bassoon with a harpsichord or organ realising the chords from a figured bass, and this has disappeared entirely by the Classical period. Melodically, Baroque lines tend to be long, spun out and heavily ornamented, unfolding continuously, whereas Classical melodies are balanced and periodic, built from tidy phrases that answer one another. Harmonically the Baroque drives forward with strong sequences and frequent movement, while Classical harmony is simpler and slower-moving, which leaves the melody exposed. The keyboard instrument changes from harpsichord to piano, and the orchestra changes from mostly strings and continuo to a standardised body of strings, pairs of woodwind, horns, trumpets and timpani, with the clarinet arriving in the Classical period.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The six elements, side by side:**

| Element | Baroque | Classical |
|---|---|---|
| Texture | polyphonic, contrapuntal | homophonic, often with an **Alberti bass** |
| Dynamics | **terraced**, sudden steps | **crescendo and diminuendo** |
| Continuo | **basso continuo** with figured bass | none |
| Melody | long, spun out, ornamented | balanced, periodic, answering phrases |
| Harmony | driving, strong sequences | simpler, slower-moving |
| Keyboard | **harpsichord** | **piano** |

**And the orchestra**: mostly strings plus continuo, becoming a standardised body of strings, **pairs** of woodwind, horns, trumpets and timpani — with the **clarinet** a Classical arrival.

**To reach the top band**, take each element **in turn across both styles**, rather than describing one period and then the other. That is what makes a comparison rather than two descriptions.

questions.prompt: Explain how the change from harpsichord to piano helps to account for the other differences between Baroque and Classical style.
questions.solution: The harpsichord sounds its strings by plucking them with a quill, and a quill plucks with the same force however hard the key is pressed. A player therefore cannot make a note louder by pressing harder, and gradual dynamics are physically impossible. To change volume the player must change manual or add a stop, which produces a sudden step rather than a gradual change, and this is precisely what terraced dynamics are. Baroque dynamic practice is therefore partly a consequence of what the instrument could do. Around 1700 Bartolomeo Cristofori built a keyboard in which hammers strike the strings and fall away, so that a harder touch produces a louder note. Its name, pianoforte, means soft loud, and describes exactly the capability the harpsichord lacked. Once a keyboard could grow and fade, composers began to write music that grows and fades, and the texture that benefits most from this is one with a single singing melody on top which can be shaped expressively, supported by an accompaniment beneath. The piano and homophonic texture therefore arrive together, and counterpoint of equal independent lines becomes less central. The continuo disappears for a related reason: once the harmony is written into the parts themselves, for example as an Alberti bass or as sustained wind chords, there is nothing left for a continuo to fill in, so it becomes redundant rather than unfashionable. Finally, the forms change because the available contrasts change. Ritornello form is built on the contrast between few players and many, which was the strongest contrast available when dynamics were terraced, whereas sonata form is built on contrast of key and theme, which suits a texture with a clear melody.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The chain runs: instrument, then dynamics, then texture, then form.**

1. **The harpsichord plucks.** A quill plucks with the **same force however hard you press**, so touch cannot change the volume and a crescendo is impossible. Getting louder means changing manual or stop — a **sudden step**. That *is* terraced dynamics.
2. **The piano strikes.** Cristofori's hammer action, from around 1700, makes a harder touch give a louder note. Its name, **pianoforte**, means *soft-loud* — exactly what the harpsichord could not do.
3. **So the texture changed.** The texture that benefits most from gradual dynamics is one with a **single singing melody on top** that can be shaped. The piano and **homophony** arrive together.
4. **The continuo became redundant.** Once the harmony is written into the parts — an Alberti bass, sustained wind chords — there is nothing for a continuo to fill in.
5. **So the forms changed.** **Ritornello form** is built on the contrast of **few players against many**, the strongest contrast available under terraced dynamics. **Sonata form** is built on contrast of **key and theme**, which suits the new texture.

**The point that earns the top band** is the causal chain itself: the forms changed because the available contrasts changed.

questions.prompt: Explain why wider listening matters for this area of study, and describe how you would work out the style of an unfamiliar piece in the exam.
questions.solution: Wider listening matters because two questions in the paper are about music you have never heard. One question in Section A is on an unfamiliar piece with a skeleton score, asking about its musical elements, contexts and language, and the extended response in Section B asks for a comparison between a set work and an unfamiliar piece from the same area of study. Neither can be revised directly, so the only preparation possible is to know the style well enough that an unfamiliar example in it holds no surprises. Pearson suggests four wider listening pieces for this area of study, Handel's Concerto Grosso op 6 no. 5, Vivaldi's Winter from The Four Seasons, Mozart's Piano Sonata in C K.545 and Haydn's English Sonata, and although these are suggestions rather than compulsory, they are chosen to cover the concerto grosso, the solo concerto, sonata form and rondo form, which between them are the ground the two set works do not cover. Faced with an unfamiliar piece I would work in a fixed order. First I would listen for a basso continuo, because a harpsichord or organ filling in chords under a bass line means Baroque. Second I would listen to the dynamics, since terraced steps mean Baroque and a crescendo means Classical. These two usually settle the question between them. Third I would consider the texture, contrapuntal suggesting Baroque and melody with accompaniment suggesting Classical, and fourth the keyboard instrument. I would then write what I actually heard and say what it indicates, rather than naming a period and hoping, because the marks are for the evidence as much as for the conclusion.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Why it matters.** Two questions are on music you have never heard:

- **Section A** has one question on an **unfamiliar piece** with a skeleton score, on its musical elements, contexts and language.
- **Section B** is an extended **comparison of a set work with an unfamiliar piece from the same area of study**.

Neither can be revised directly. The only preparation is to know the **style** so well that an unfamiliar example holds no surprises. That is what wider listening is for, and the specification requires it for **every** area of study.

**The four suggested pieces here** — Handel's *Concerto Grosso op 6 no. 5*, Vivaldi's *Winter*, Mozart's **K.545**, Haydn's *English Sonata* — cover the **concerto grosso**, the **solo concerto**, **sonata form** and **rondo**: the ground the two set works do not.

**The order to work in:**

1. **Is there a continuo?** A harpsichord or organ under a bass line means **Baroque**.
2. **Are the dynamics terraced or gradual?** Steps mean **Baroque**; a crescendo means **Classical**.
3. **What is the texture?** Contrapuntal suggests Baroque; melody and accompaniment suggests Classical.
4. **Which keyboard?** Harpsichord or piano.

The first two usually settle it. **Then write the evidence**, not just the conclusion: *a harpsichord realising a figured bass, so this is Baroque*. The marks are for what you heard as much as for the label you give it.

examTechnique.body:
For an unfamiliar piece, check for a continuo first and the dynamics second, since those two usually settle the period.

Write down what you heard and say what it indicates, rather than naming a period without evidence.

Distinguish a sonata, which is a piece, from sonata form, which is the shape of one movement.

Remember that in the recapitulation both subjects are in the tonic.

Separate rondo from ritornello by asking whether the recurring section changes key.

In a comparison, take each element in turn across both pieces rather than describing one piece and then the other.

Use the correct terms: concertino and ripieno, basso continuo, figured bass, terraced dynamics, Alberti bass.
examinerErrors: Confusing a sonata with sonata form.
Saying the recapitulation keeps the second subject in the dominant.
Calling a ritornello a rondo, or the reverse.
Putting a clarinet in a Baroque orchestra.
Saying the continuo went out of fashion, rather than becoming redundant.
Naming a period for an unfamiliar piece without giving the evidence for it.
Describing two pieces separately when the question asks for a comparison.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer does not recite a table of differences: it explains them. It knows the harpsichord's mechanism is why Baroque dynamics are terraced, that the piano and homophonic texture arrive together because a singing melody is what gradual dynamics are for, and that the continuo became redundant once the harmony was written into the parts. It can say why ritornello form suits an age of terraced dynamics and sonata form does not. Faced with an unfamiliar piece it works in a fixed order and writes down the evidence, not just the conclusion. And in a comparison it takes one element at a time across both works, which is what turns two descriptions into an answer.
